title: Integral Probability Boundaries
claim: A standard single-number metric gives loose linear bounds, while our non-linear boundary traces the exact achievable region tightly, especially at the extremes.
layout: single square plot, lens-shaped curve between diagonal, grey tangent lines versus blue contour
description: A single square plot with both axes running from 0 to 1. The x-axis is labelled E_Q[f]. The y-axis labels are clipped at the left edge. Light dashed grid lines and a dashed grey diagonal run from (0,0) to (1,1). A thick blue lens-shaped contour sits around the diagonal. Its upper arc rises steeply from the origin and flattens near (1,1). Its lower arc mirrors it, hugging the bottom edge before curving up sharply at the right. Two thick light-grey straight lines, parallel to the diagonal, touch the blue lens at one tangent point each. One lies above the lens and one below. They show the loose linear bounds from a standard metric. The gap between each grey line and the blue curve is the improvement, and it grows toward the corners. The eye goes first to the blue lens. The crop also shows the start of body text, 'Definition 1.1', at the bottom.
caption: Integral Probability Boundaries (IPBs) characterize the difference in expectations of any function from a given class $\F$ under two distributions $P$ and $Q$ more precisely than a standard Integral Probability Metric (IPM). We show the tight IPBs and IPM for $P \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ and $Q \sim \mathcal{N}(1, 1)$ over the set of all bounded functions where the IPM is given by the TV distance $\delta = D_\mathsf{TV}(P, Q)$, and the IPB is given by the ROC of the Neyman--Pearson test (see [ref]). We show IPM-based bounds with grey lines ( –), and IPB-based bounds that trace the contour of the achievable region $\C_\F(P \| Q)$ with blue lines ( –).
abstract: Bounds based on Integral Probability Metrics (IPMs) are ubiquitous in machine learning and statistics, appearing, e.g., in generalization, alignment, fairness, and privacy. IPMs reduce the discrepancy between two distributions to a single worst-case gap between expectations. This compression is costly: for rare events, safety failures, or under-represented groups, IPM-based bounds are loose or vacuous. We introduce a non-linear generalization of IPMs, which we term Integral Probability Boundaries (IPBs). Unlike IPMs, IPBs provide bounds that are tight at the extremes. We derive their basic properties and present algorithms for estimating them in practically relevant settings. We demonstrate the usage of IPBs in both theoretical and practical applications for alignment, judge-free performance estimation, and fairness, where they enable us to obtain sharp bounds on performance and fairness gaps, e.g., 15 p.p. more precise estimates on fairness gaps for rare groups in a realistic generative modeling task, compared to the state of the art.
